body:
How much SEO services cost in 2026: what the price includes and why it differs so much. The short answer is that there is no single rate, because the price depends on the number of pages, on the competition in your industry and on how much of the work actually stays on the agency's side.

Below we explain what the price is made of in practice and which pricing models you will meet on the market. You won't find made-up figures here, but the real factors that determine them.

How much SEO services cost in 2026: what the price includes and why it differs so much

An offer for SEO services seems, at first glance, hard to compare with another, because each agency groups the same activities differently. The sections below break the price down by component, then by the factors that push it up or down.

Our current figures are on the page with SEO optimization prices, updated directly by the team, not estimated in this article.

Market prices vary so much between agencies precisely because the term "SEO services" can mean, in practice, anything from a single audit sent once a year to a full team working on the site every month. Without knowing exactly which activities are included, the final figure on an offer says very little about what you get in return.

What the price of an SEO service actually includes

How much SEO services cost only becomes visible once you break the price down by component, not from a single monthly figure. A serious SEO optimization offer usually covers four areas of work, each with a real cost in working hours.

  • The technical side: speed, indexing, URL structure, fixing crawl errors, usually grouped under technical SEO. This also covers the periodic check of wrong response codes and of pages that end up, by mistake, outside Google's index.
  • Content: keyword research, new articles, updating older pages. A serious agency doesn't write just any text on any topic, but starts from a clear brief about what your audience is searching for.
  • External authority: obtaining relevant links through link building, usually the slowest and most expensive component in the long run. A single link earned from a relevant site often takes more work than a whole blog article.
  • Reporting and analysis: measuring results and explaining them to you, in a clear periodic report, not a simple export of figures. A good report ties every figure to a concrete action taken that month, not just to a rising chart.

A low price almost always excludes one of these areas, most often link building, because it takes the most manual work relative to the result obtained. When an offer looks unusually good, ask directly which of the four areas is missing from the package.

Why prices differ so much between agencies

Two offers for the same site can differ greatly, and the reason is not always the quality of the work. A few factors explain most of the difference.

  • The number of pages to optimize: a site with a few dozen pages takes much less time than a store with thousands of product pages, where every category and every filter can become an entry page from search.
  • The competition in your industry: a crowded market, with competitors who constantly invest in content and links, demands a more sustained pace of work just to keep the positions you have already won, not only to climb.
  • What you already do in-house: if you already have a writer or a developer who handles the technical side, the agency bills only for the rest of the work, and the price drops in proportion to what is left to do.
  • The target geographic area: local SEO, for a single city, takes a different amount of work than national SEO, across dozens of cities at once, where each area has its own searches and its own local competition.
  • The urgency required: quickly recovering a lost position takes resources concentrated in a short time, not the usual monthly pace, and this concentrated effort is reflected directly in the price.

For this reason, compare offers on their content, not just on the final figure. Two agencies can bill similar amounts for very different amounts of real work, and the difference only comes to light after a few months of collaboration, when the first report shows what was actually done.

The pricing models you will meet on the market

Besides the amount billed, how it is calculated also matters. On the Romanian market there are mainly three models, each suited to a different stage of the collaboration between you and the agency.

The fixed monthly retainer

The most common model for ongoing background work: the same package of activities, billed monthly, no matter how many hours it actually takes in a busier month. It works well for a stable site with clear long-term goals, where the pace of work stays constant from one month to the next.

The risk with this model appears when the package stays the same year after year, even though the site has grown or the competition has intensified. Ask for a periodic review of the package, not just an invoice that repeats automatically.

Project-based pricing

Suited to work with a clear end: a migration with no loss in Google, a full technical audit or rebuilding the internal link architecture. The price is set once, based on the estimated volume of work, not monthly.

This model works well when you can describe exactly what must be delivered at the end, for example an audit report with a list of fixes. It doesn't suit ongoing background work, where the real volume varies from one month to the next.

Hourly consulting

The most flexible option, useful for companies that already have an in-house team and only need targeted guidance or a periodic audit, not ongoing execution. It usually costs more per hour than a retainer, precisely because it doesn't involve a monthly commitment.

It makes the most sense for companies that want to check, from time to time, whether the in-house team is working correctly, not for those that have nobody to put the recommendations into practice.

Signs that a low price hides risks

A price well below the market does not automatically mean a good offer. It usually hides one of the situations below.

  • Guaranteed positions in Google: nobody controls the ranking algorithm, and a firm promise of this kind is a warning sign, not a sign of trust.
  • Reports without substance: general figures, with no direct link to your site's pages and keywords, hard to verify for someone who doesn't already work in the field.
  • Low-quality links obtained in bulk: they can bring a temporary increase, followed by a penalty that is hard to fix, sometimes months after they were placed.
  • Generic content, not written for your business: recycled texts, with no connection to your real products or services, that don't answer your customers' concrete questions.

A serious initial SEO audit, with concrete findings about your site, is the easiest sign to check before signing. If the proposal you receive could be sent, unchanged, to any other company in any other industry, it did not start from a real analysis of your site.

How to set the right budget for your business

The right budget starts from the goal, not from the lowest offer received. A new site, with no history, needs a bigger initial effort on the technical and content side, before links and authority really matter.

For an online store with thousands of product pages, the budget usually follows the number of pages to optimize, not just the traffic goal. For a local business with a single location, a package focused on local SEO usually costs less than a nationwide campaign, precisely because the coverage area is smaller.

The portfolio of projects completed previously shows the type of site the agency has already worked on, a useful reference when you compare the size of your project with the agency's real experience.

A practical rule, valid in any industry: allocate the budget first to the technical and content side, because without them the links obtained later have no authority to pass on. Only after these two areas are in order does increasing the link building budget usually bring a visible effect.

What to ask an agency before you sign

Google Search Central publishes a list of useful recommendations before hiring an SEO specialist, which also apply to the Romanian market. The official document Do you need an SEO? stresses transparency about the way of working, not just the promised result.

  • Which concrete activities are included in the monthly price and which are billed separately.
  • Who remains the owner of the accounts, for example Google Search Console and Analytics, after the collaboration ends.
  • What reporting you get and at what interval, and who explains the results, not just who emails them.
  • What happens to the content already published if you end the collaboration.
  • How long it usually takes for the first visible effects to appear on the tracked keywords.

The answers to these questions matter as much as the price itself, because they show whether you are left with something concrete at the end of the collaboration. An agency that avoids answering any of them clearly deserves a further conversation before you sign, not necessarily an automatic rejection.

How much SEO services cost remains, in the end, a question with an individual answer, tied to your site and your concrete goals, not to a fixed figure valid for any business.
